title: General Ichthyology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Ichthyology curriculum: fish classification (Agnatha, Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes), external and internal morphology, scales, fins, gill/respiratory structure, circulatory and digestive systems, swim bladder, sensory systems (lateral line), osmoregulation, and reproduction, illustrated with common Nigerian fish species.

questions.question: Ichthyology is best defined as the branch of zoology concerned with:
options: The study of freshwater invertebrates only
questions.explanation: Ichthyology is the branch of zoology devoted to the taxonomy, anatomy, physiology, ecology, and behaviour of fishes.

questions.question: Fishes are broadly classified into three major taxonomic groups based on skeletal composition and jaw structure. Which of these is one of them?
questions.explanation: The three superclasses/classes of fishes are Agnatha (jawless fishes), Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes), and Osteichthyes (bony fishes).

questions.question: Which class of fishes is characterized by a cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scales, and the absence of a swim bladder?
questions.explanation: Chondrichthyes (sharks, rays, and skates) have skeletons made of cartilage rather than bone, placoid (dermal denticle) scales, and lack a swim bladder.

questions.question: The class Osteichthyes, to which most Nigerian food fishes belong, is defined by which key feature?
options: A skeleton composed largely of true bone
A skeleton composed entirely of cartilage
The complete absence of a skeleton
questions.correct_answer: A skeleton composed largely of true bone
questions.explanation: Osteichthyes, the bony fishes, possess a skeleton of ossified bone, distinguishing them from the cartilaginous Chondrichthyes.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an agnathan (jawless fish)?
questions.explanation: Lampreys, along with hagfishes, are jawless fishes belonging to the group Agnatha, lacking true jaws unlike all other fish classes.

questions.question: The African catfish, Clarias gariepinus, belongs to which fish family?
questions.explanation: Clarias gariepinus belongs to the family Clariidae, the air-breathing catfishes, which possess accessory air-breathing organs.

questions.question: Tilapia species (e.g. Oreochromis niloticus) belong to which fish family?
questions.explanation: Tilapias are members of the family Cichlidae, characterized by a single nostril on each side and mouthbrooding behaviour in many species.

questions.question: The external body shape of a fish adapted for fast, sustained swimming in open water (e.g. tuna) is termed:
questions.explanation: A fusiform (torpedo-shaped) body reduces drag and is typical of fast-swimming pelagic fishes such as tuna and mackerel.

questions.question: An eel-like, elongated body shape in fish is described as:
questions.explanation: Anguilliform describes a long, snake-like body form typical of eels, allowing lateral undulatory swimming through tight spaces.

questions.question: The paired fins of a fish that correspond to the forelimbs of tetrapods are the:
questions.explanation: Pectoral fins are paired fins located just behind the head and are homologous to the forelimbs of terrestrial vertebrates.

questions.question: Which unpaired fin is located on the dorsal (upper) surface of a fish's body?
questions.explanation: The dorsal fin runs along the fish's back and helps stabilize the body against rolling during swimming.

questions.question: The caudal fin of a fish primarily functions to:
options: Provide the main propulsive force for forward swimming
questions.correct_answer: Provide the main propulsive force for forward swimming
questions.explanation: The caudal (tail) fin generates most of the thrust that propels a fish forward through lateral undulation of the body.

questions.question: A homocercal caudal fin, found in most bony fishes, is characterized by:
options: External symmetry with the vertebral column ending near the fin's base, not extending into the upper lobe
The vertebral column extending into an elongated upper lobe only
Complete absence of a tail fin
questions.correct_answer: External symmetry with the vertebral column ending near the fin's base, not extending into the upper lobe
questions.explanation: In a homocercal tail, typical of most teleosts, the fin appears externally symmetrical even though the vertebral column turns upward internally.

questions.question: The heterocercal caudal fin, in which the vertebral column extends into an enlarged upper lobe, is typical of which group?
questions.explanation: Sharks and many other cartilaginous fishes have a heterocercal tail, where the upper lobe is larger because the vertebral column extends into it.

questions.question: Fish scales that are thin, rounded, and overlap like roof shingles, common in soft-rayed fishes such as tilapia, are called:
questions.explanation: Cycloid scales have smooth, rounded posterior edges and are common in many soft-rayed teleost fishes.

questions.question: Ctenoid scales differ from cycloid scales mainly by having:
options: Tiny comb-like projections (ctenii) along their posterior edge
A cartilaginous rather than bony composition
questions.correct_answer: Tiny comb-like projections (ctenii) along their posterior edge
questions.explanation: Ctenoid scales bear small comb-like spines (ctenii) on their exposed edge, unlike the smooth-edged cycloid scales.

questions.question: The tooth-like structures covering the skin of sharks and rays, which give their skin a rough, sandpaper-like texture, are called:
questions.explanation: Placoid scales, or dermal denticles, are small, tooth-like structures unique to cartilaginous fishes, giving shark skin its characteristic roughness.

questions.question: Age determination in bony fish is commonly done by counting growth rings (annuli) on which structure?
questions.explanation: Scales and otoliths (ear bones) deposit concentric growth rings that reflect seasonal growth variation, enabling age estimation.

questions.question: The primary respiratory organs of most fishes, responsible for gas exchange with water, are the:
questions.explanation: Gills are highly vascularized structures that extract dissolved oxygen from water and release carbon dioxide, serving as the main respiratory organ in fish.

questions.question: Water flow over the gills and blood flow within the gill lamellae typically move in opposite directions. This arrangement is called:
questions.explanation: Countercurrent flow between water and blood across the gill lamellae maximizes oxygen diffusion efficiency compared to a concurrent arrangement.

questions.question: Clarias gariepinus (African catfish) can survive in poorly oxygenated water because it possesses:
options: An accessory air-breathing organ (arborescent organ) allowing it to breathe atmospheric air
Lungs identical to those of mammals
A swim bladder used for respiration only
questions.correct_answer: An accessory air-breathing organ (arborescent organ) allowing it to breathe atmospheric air
questions.explanation: Clariid catfishes possess a branched, vascularized suprabranchial (arborescent) organ that lets them gulp atmospheric air, enabling survival in hypoxic waters.

questions.question: The chamber covering and protecting the gills on each side of a bony fish's head is the:
questions.explanation: The operculum is a bony flap that covers and protects the gills and also assists in pumping water over the gill filaments.

questions.question: The two-chambered fish heart consists of which structures, arranged in series?
options: A single atrium and a single ventricle
Two atria and two ventricles like mammals
questions.correct_answer: A single atrium and a single ventricle
questions.explanation: Fish have a simple two-chambered heart, an atrium and a ventricle, that pumps deoxygenated blood forward to the gills in a single circulatory loop.

questions.question: Fish circulation is described as 'single circuit' because:
options: Blood passes through the heart once per complete circulation around the body
Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit
Blood never returns to the heart
questions.correct_answer: Blood passes through the heart once per complete circulation around the body
questions.explanation: In fish, blood flows from the heart to the gills, then to the body, and back to the heart only once per full circuit, unlike the double circulation in mammals.

questions.question: The gas-filled internal organ that helps many bony fishes regulate buoyancy is the:
questions.explanation: The swim bladder is a gas-filled sac that allows bony fish to adjust their buoyancy, remaining neutrally buoyant at different depths without constant swimming effort.

questions.question: In a 'physostomous' swim bladder, gas is regulated via:
options: A duct (pneumatic duct) connecting the swim bladder to the oesophagus or gut
A completely closed system with no duct
questions.correct_answer: A duct (pneumatic duct) connecting the swim bladder to the oesophagus or gut
questions.explanation: Physostomous fishes (e.g. many catfishes and cyprinids) have a pneumatic duct linking the swim bladder to the gut, allowing gas to be gulped or released directly.

questions.question: A 'physoclistous' swim bladder differs from a physostomous one in that it:
options: Has no duct to the gut; gas is regulated via the gas gland and oval organ into the bloodstream
Is always absent in bony fish
Is filled with water instead of gas
Is found only in cartilaginous fish
questions.correct_answer: Has no duct to the gut; gas is regulated via the gas gland and oval organ into the bloodstream
questions.explanation: Physoclistous fishes lack a pneumatic duct and instead regulate swim bladder gas volume internally through specialized glands that secrete or absorb gas via the blood.

questions.question: The fish digestive organ responsible for the initial chemical breakdown of food using acid and enzymes is the:
questions.explanation: The stomach secretes acid and digestive enzymes (e.g. pepsin) to begin the chemical breakdown of ingested food before it passes to the intestine.

questions.question: Finger-like pouches found near the junction of the stomach and intestine in many teleost fish, which increase the surface area for digestion and absorption, are called:
questions.explanation: Pyloric caeca are blind sac-like extensions near the pylorus that increase digestive and absorptive surface area, and their number varies by species.

questions.question: The relative length of a fish's intestine generally correlates with its diet such that:
options: Herbivorous fish tend to have longer intestines than carnivorous fish
Carnivorous fish always have longer intestines than herbivores
Intestine length is unrelated to diet in fish
All fish have identical intestine lengths regardless of diet
questions.correct_answer: Herbivorous fish tend to have longer intestines than carnivorous fish
questions.explanation: Plant material is harder to digest, so herbivorous and omnivorous fish typically have proportionally longer intestines than carnivorous species that eat easily digested animal protein.

questions.question: The sensory system unique to fish (and some aquatic amphibians) that detects water movement, vibration, and pressure changes is the:
questions.explanation: The lateral line is a row of mechanoreceptors (neuromasts) along a fish's body that senses water displacement, helping detect prey, predators, and obstacles.

questions.question: Barbels, the whisker-like sensory organs found around the mouth of catfishes, primarily function to:
options: Detect food by touch and taste, especially in murky or dark water
questions.correct_answer: Detect food by touch and taste, especially in murky or dark water
questions.explanation: Barbels are covered with taste buds and tactile receptors, helping bottom-dwelling and nocturnal fish like catfish locate food in low-visibility environments.

questions.question: Osmoregulation in fish refers to the process by which fish:
options: Maintain the proper balance of water and salts (ions) within their body fluids
Control the rate of their heartbeat
questions.correct_answer: Maintain the proper balance of water and salts (ions) within their body fluids
questions.explanation: Osmoregulation involves controlling the internal concentration of water and dissolved ions, critical because fish live in environments with different salinities than their body fluids.

questions.question: A freshwater bony fish, whose body fluids are hyperosmotic (saltier) relative to its surrounding water, must primarily deal with:
options: Constant water influx and the need to excrete large volumes of dilute urine
Constant water loss to the environment
Excess salt intake through the gills
questions.correct_answer: Constant water influx and the need to excrete large volumes of dilute urine
questions.explanation: In freshwater, water tends to enter the fish's body by osmosis, so freshwater fish drink little and excrete large amounts of dilute urine to eliminate excess water.

questions.question: A marine bony fish, whose body fluids are hypoosmotic (less salty) relative to seawater, compensates for water loss mainly by:
options: Drinking seawater and actively excreting excess salt through the gills
Producing large volumes of dilute urine
Absorbing salt through its skin only
questions.correct_answer: Drinking seawater and actively excreting excess salt through the gills
questions.explanation: Marine teleosts lose water osmotically to the saltier sea, so they drink seawater to replace it and use specialized chloride cells in the gills to excrete the excess salt absorbed.

questions.question: Most fish reproduce via which mode of fertilization?
options: External fertilization, where eggs and sperm are released into the water
questions.correct_answer: External fertilization, where eggs and sperm are released into the water
questions.explanation: The majority of fish species are oviparous with external fertilization, releasing eggs and milt (sperm) into the water where fertilization occurs.

questions.question: Mouthbrooding, a reproductive strategy seen in many tilapia species, involves:
options: A parent holding fertilized eggs and/or young in its mouth for protection until they can fend for themselves
Laying eggs that hatch instantly outside the body
Live birth of fully developed young
Eggs being buried permanently in sand
questions.correct_answer: A parent holding fertilized eggs and/or young in its mouth for protection until they can fend for themselves
questions.explanation: Mouthbrooding cichlids, including many Oreochromis species, incubate and protect their eggs and fry inside the parent's mouth, improving offspring survival.

questions.question: Fecundity in fish biology refers to:
options: The number of eggs produced by a female fish, usually per spawning season
The age at which a fish reaches sexual maturity
The length of a fish at first capture
The number of fin rays a fish possesses
questions.correct_answer: The number of eggs produced by a female fish, usually per spawning season
questions.explanation: Fecundity is a measure of reproductive potential, quantified as the number of eggs a female produces, which varies widely among species and with body size.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the lateral line's role in schooling behaviour of fish?
options: It helps fish detect the movement and position of neighbouring fish to maintain coordinated schools
It has no role in schooling
It regulates the fish's body temperature during schooling
questions.correct_answer: It helps fish detect the movement and position of neighbouring fish to maintain coordinated schools
questions.explanation: By sensing water displacement from nearby fish, the lateral line allows individuals to synchronize movement and maintain spacing within a school.

questions.question: In fish gill anatomy, the primary site of gas exchange is the:
options: Gill lamellae (secondary lamellae on the gill filaments)
questions.correct_answer: Gill lamellae (secondary lamellae on the gill filaments)
questions.explanation: Thin, richly vascularized secondary lamellae projecting from the gill filaments provide the large surface area where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the water.

questions.question: Gill rakers, bony projections on the gill arches, primarily function to:
options: Strain food particles or protect the delicate gill filaments from damage
questions.correct_answer: Strain food particles or protect the delicate gill filaments from damage
questions.explanation: Gill rakers act as a sieve to filter food items (especially in filter-feeding fish) and shield the fragile gill filaments from abrasive particles.

questions.question: Which of the following fish species is an example of an obligate air-breather commonly farmed and found in Nigerian waters?
questions.explanation: Heterotis niloticus (the African bonytongue) possesses a modified swim bladder used as an accessory respiratory organ, allowing it to breathe atmospheric air.

questions.question: In fish taxonomy, the correct hierarchical order (from broadest to most specific) is:
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Phylum, Kingdom, Order, Class, Family, Genus, Species
Class, Kingdom, Phylum, Family, Order, Genus, Species
questions.correct_answer: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
questions.explanation: Standard biological (Linnaean) classification proceeds from the broadest category, Kingdom, down through Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, to the most specific rank, Species.

questions.question: The scientific (binomial) name of the Nile tilapia is:
questions.explanation: Oreochromis niloticus is the correct binomial name for the Nile tilapia, one of the most widely cultured fish species in Africa.

questions.question: The kidneys of fish primarily function in osmoregulation and excretion by:
options: Filtering blood to remove metabolic wastes and regulate water/salt balance
questions.correct_answer: Filtering blood to remove metabolic wastes and regulate water/salt balance
questions.explanation: Fish kidneys filter nitrogenous wastes (mainly ammonia) from the blood and play a central role, alongside the gills, in maintaining osmotic balance.
